fetched_contents.text: DISCOVER: Automated Curricula for Sparse-Reward Reinforcement Learning Leander Diaz‐Bone ,1 Marco Bagatella11footnotemark: 1 ,1,2 Jonas Hübotter11footnotemark: 1 ,1 Andreas Krause1 1ETH Zürich, Switzerland 2Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems, Germany Abstract Sparse-reward reinforcement learning (RL) can model a wide range of highly complex tasks. Solving sparse-reward tasks is RL’s core premise—requiring efficient exploration coupled with long-horizon credit assignment—and overcoming these challenges is key for building self-improving agents with superhuman ability. Prior work commonly explores with the objective of solving many sparse-reward tasks, making exploration of individual high-dimensional, long-horizon tasks intractable. We argue that solving such challenging tasks requires solving simpler tasks that are relevant to the target task, i.e., whose achieval will teach the agent skills required for solving the target task. We demonstrate that this sense of direction, necessary for effective exploration, can be extracted from existing RL algorithms, without leveraging any prior information. To this end, we propose a method for directed sparse-reward goal-conditioned very long-horizon RL (DISCOVER), which selects exploratory goals in the direction of the target task. We connect DISCOVER to principled exploration in bandits, formally bounding the time until the target task becomes achievable in terms of the agent’s initial distance to the target, but independent of the volume of the space of all tasks. We then perform a thorough evaluation in high-dimensional environments. Although RL has led to breakthroughs in many domains such as Atari games [45], board games [e.g., 66], and reasoning [26], sparse-reward problems, in which a reward is only observed once the task is completed, remain very challenging [38, 80]. These sparse-reward tasks are hard to solve as the agent needs to gain a deep understanding of the environment without ever observing a reward. As such, and since they are naturally defined without any human supervision, solving sparse-reward tasks is one of the core premises of RL. We focus on the setting where the agent is given a single sparse-reward problem to solve. In sparse-reward RL, traditional methods from RL fail as they need to randomly observe the reward signal to make progress, which becomes exceedingly unlikely in long-horizon tasks [e.g., 49, 87]. One technique for overcoming this challenge is to frame sparse-reward tasks as multi-goal problems, which enables the agent to learn about harder goals by generalizing from already learned simpler goals [63, 5]. In this framework, a goal needs to be specified for the policy in each episode. This goal selection step plays a crucial role in guiding the exploration of the agent [53]. Choosing a goal essentially presents its own exploration-exploitation dilemma at a higher level of abstraction: should the agent try to pursue its final goal or rather aim to reach novel, but achievable intermediate goals, expanding its horizon of expertise? Previously introduced goal selection strategies have focused largely on either exploration [e.g., 53] or exploitation [5]. In this work, we argue that goal selection should naturally address this trade-off, considering both the novelty of commanded goals, and thus their exploration potential, as well as their relevance to the final objective, while considering their achievability. We propose DISCOVER, a method for effectively balancing achievability, relevance, and novelty during goal selection. We find that these quantities can be estimated by commonly used critic networks in standard deep RL algorithms. We learn an ensemble of critics to estimate the agent’s uncertainty about the direction of the final task. Intuitively, DISCOVER leverages these value estimates to determine which intermediate goals are most useful towards learning to solve the final task. We find that DISCOVER enables RL agents to solve substantially more challenging tasks than previous exploration strategies in RL. Unlike bounds in prior work, our bound for DISCOVER is independent of the volume of the space of all goals and depends linearly on the “shortest distance” between the agent’s initial state and the state at which the final task is achieved. fetched_contents.text: Constraint-Aware Reinforcement Learning via Adaptive Action Scaling \NameUsama Ahmed Siddiquie \Emails46usidd@uni-bonn.de \NameShahram Khorshidi \Emailkhorshidi@cs.uni-bonn.de \NameMaren Bennewitz \Emailmaren@cs.uni-bonn.de \addrHumanoid Robots Lab University of Bonn Germany Abstract Safe reinforcement learning (RL) seeks to mitigate unsafe behaviors that arise from exploration during training by reducing constraint violations while maintaining task performance. Existing approaches typically rely on a single policy to jointly optimize reward and safety, which can cause instability due to conflicting objectives, or they use external safety filters that override actions and require prior system knowledge. In this paper, we propose a modular cost-aware regulator that scales the agent’s actions based on predicted constraint violations, preserving exploration through smooth action modulation rather than overriding the policy. The regulator is trained to minimize constraint violations while avoiding degenerate suppression of actions. Our approach integrates seamlessly with off-policy RL methods such as SAC and TD3, and achieves state-of-the-art return-to-cost ratios on Safety Gym locomotion tasks with sparse costs, reducing constraint violations by up to 126 times while increasing returns by over an order of magnitude compared to prior methods. 1 Introduction Reinforcement Learning (RL) has demonstrated remarkable success across a range of domains, including Atari games [mnih2015human], robotics [gu2017deep, wu2023daydreamer], and long-horizon strategy games [silver2017mastering, vinyals2019grandmaster]. This success is significantly facilitated by exploratory behavior, which allows agents to discover effective behaviors. However, such exploratory behaviors often lead to the violation of system constraints. While such violations are tolerable in simulation and games with free resets, they pose serious risks in real-world applications [amodei2016concrete]. Violating safety constraints can lead to irreversible damage or system failure. To address this issue, Safe Reinforcement Learning (Safe RL) [garcia2015comprehensive] aims to minimize constraint violations during both training and deployment. Safe RL methods can be broadly categorized into two groups: safe exploration and constrained RL. Safe exploration techniques aim to prevent the agent from taking actions that violate safety constraints. These methods typically rely on prior knowledge of the system dynamics and feasible safe states to construct control barrier functions [ames2019control, dai2023safe, zhang2023spatial], or model predictive shields [banerjee2024dynamic, dawood2025l4dc, agha2024exploring]. Although effective, their applicability is limited by the need for detailed prior information about the system dynamics, an assumption that often does not hold in early learning stages or tasks where system dynamics are unknown. Constrained RL allows the agent to learn both reward and cost signals online, without requiring knowledge of the system dynamics. The agent is trained to maximize cumulative rewards while minimizing constraint violations. Common approaches include Lagrangian-based methods [achiam2017constrained, tessler2018reward, ray2019benchmarking, stooke2020responsive], and budget-based methods [sootla2022saute, sootla2022enhancing]. However, a core limitation of these methods is the difficulty of balancing reward and cost within a single policy. Conflicting gradients can cause the agent to behave either too conservatively or unsafely, leading to instability, constraint violations, or poor performance [stooke2020responsive, navon2022multi]. The regulator applies element-wise scaling to attenuate risky actions, enforcing safety without requiring prior knowledge of dynamics or compromising exploration. Although our approach resembles safe exploration in formulation, we do not require prior knowledge of the system dynamics, and we do not override the task agent’s actions, thereby preserving both exploration and safety without external overrides. We evaluate our approach on several dynamical systems from Safety Gymnasium [ji2023safety]. Offline reinforcement learning (RL) enables policy learning from pre-collected datasets, avoiding costly and risky online interactions, but it often struggles with long-horizon tasks involving sparse rewards. Existing goal-conditioned and hierarchical offline RL methods decompose such tasks and generate intermediate rewards to mitigate limitations of traditional offline RL, but usually overlook temporal dependencies among subgoals and rely on imprecise reward shaping, leading to suboptimal policies. To address these issues, we propose STO-RL (Offline RL using LLM-Guided Subgoal Temporal Order), an offline RL framework that leverages large language models (LLMs) to generate temporally ordered subgoal sequences and corresponding state-to-subgoal-stage mappings. Using this temporal structure, STO-RL applies potential-based reward shaping to transform sparse terminal rewards into dense, temporally consistent signals, promoting subgoal progress while avoiding suboptimal solutions. The resulting augmented dataset with shaped rewards enables efficient offline training of high-performing policies. Evaluations on four discrete and continuous sparse-reward benchmarks demonstrate that STO-RL consistently outperforms state-of-the-art offline goal-conditioned and hierarchical RL baselines, achieving faster convergence, higher success rates, and shorter trajectories. Ablation studies further confirm STO-RL’s robustness to imperfect or noisy LLM-generated subgoal sequences, demonstrating that LLM-guided subgoal temporal structures combined with theoretically grounded reward shaping provide a practical and scalable solution for long-horizon offline RL. Introduction In recent years, Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for solving sequential decision-making problems, achieving remarkable success in domains ranging from game-playing (Goldwaser and Thielscher, 2020) to robotics (Nguyen and La, 2019). Despite these achievements, DRL methods usually require extensive online interaction with the environment, which can be costly, risky, or infeasible in real-world applications such as autonomous driving or medical treatment planning (Isele et al., 2018; Yauney and Shah, 2018). To overcome this limitation, offline reinforcement learning (offline RL) (Kumar et al., 2020) has been investigated, where agents learn policies entirely from pre-collected datasets without further interactions with targeting environments. However, to date offline RL faces significant challenges in long-horizon, goal-reaching tasks with sparse rewards (Wu et al., 2024), which are practical when agents interacting with the real world. In these settings, rewards are often provided only at the final state, and in limited offline datasets, the lack of intermediate feedback also hinders efficient reward propagation. These make RL agents very challenging to learn effective behaviors (Holmes and Chi, 2025; Yunis et al., 2024). To mitigate this issue, goal-conditioned offline RL extends traditional offline RL by conditioning policies or value functions on goal representations, enabling more flexible and generalizable goal-directed behaviors (Ma et al., 2022; Park et al., 2024; Ding et al., 2019). Complementarily, hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) has been proposed to tackle sparse-reward and long-horizon problems by introducing a multi-level decision-making hierarchy (Schwab and Ray, 2017; Nachum et al., 2018, 2019; Osa et al., 2019). In such a framework, a high-level policy generates subgoals to guide long-term planning, while a low-level policy learns to achieve these subgoals using primitive actions. By decomposing complex tasks into sequences of subgoal-conditioned subtasks, HRL can improve learning efficiency and exploration, but at an additional cost of algorithm design and complexity (Zhang et al., 2021). Despite these advances, both offline goal-conditioned RL and offline hierarchical RL continue to face two fundamental challenges: (1) Learning Effective Subgoals (Mesbah et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2021; Chane-Sane et al., 2021). Generating informative and achievable subgoals is critical for their success, because high-level and goal-conditioned policies rely on them to guide low-level actions toward long-horizon goals, directly influencing learning efficiency and task success. However, discovering such subgoals remains difficult due to limited data coverage, sparse rewards, and the presence of suboptimal trajectories and noisy transitions in offline datasets (Shin and Kim, 2023; Park et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023; Kujanpää et al., 2023; Rosete-Beas et al., 2023). Furthermore, existing approaches often fail to model the temporal dependencies among subgoals (Baek et al., 2025; Xu and Fekri, 2024; Ahn et al., 2025), making it challenging to learn temporally coherent subgoal sequences. This limitation leads high-level policies to generate subgoals that are inconsistent with task progression and hinder effective hierarchical coordination. (2) Reward Shaping (Mezghani et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2024; Okudo and Yamada, 2021). To alleviate the challenge of sparse rewards and enhance learning efficiency, reward shaping is commonly employed to provide denser feedback signals that guide agents toward meaningful, intermediate progress. While shaping schemes such as distance-based potential functions can introduce unintended local optima and misguide policy learning, ultimately leading to suboptimal performance (Liu et al., 2022). In this work, we identify large language model (LLM) as the critical aid, and LLM-based planning can redefine how subgoals and rewards are discovered in long-horizon, sparse-reward problems. Recent progress in sparse-reward exploration and efficient exploration methods is centered on a combination of goal-conditioned exploration, intrinsic motivation, curiosity-driven learning, and reward shaping, with recent work showing substantial improvements in sample efficiency and convergence behavior.

The most effective recent algorithms or frameworks appear to be DISCOVER and STO-RL, plus related exploration strategies such as curiosity-driven methods. DISCOVER is a goal-conditioned sparse-reward method that selects exploratory goals in the direction of the target task, rather than randomly or heuristically, and it leverages critic estimates to balance achievability, novelty, and relevance during goal selection [N1-F1]. STO-RL is a long-horizon offline sparse-reward method that uses LLM-guided subgoal temporal order and potential-based reward shaping to transform sparse terminal rewards into dense, temporally consistent signals, enabling efficient offline training and better convergence than prior goal-conditioned or hierarchical baselines [N5-F4]. In addition, the evidence points to newer curiosity-driven approaches such as CDE and CERMIC, which remove the burden of hand-designed reward models and guide exploration dynamically through intrinsic motivation or noisy surprise filtering [N6-R1][N6-R5].

The mechanisms used to guide exploration are broadly intrinsic reward shaping, curiosity, and uncertainty estimates. DISCOVER explicitly uses critic estimates of uncertainty about the direction of the final task to select goals that are both relevant and achievable [N1-F1]. STO-RL uses potential-based reward shaping to promote subgoal progress and temporally consistent reward signals [N5-F4]. Curiosity-driven methods such as CDE and CERMIC frame exploration as an intrinsic motivation problem, with CDE removing fragile reward modeling and CERMIC filtering noisy surprise signals dynamically [N6-R1][N6-R5]. The evidence also notes that exploration methods often rely on value differences between states, with one poster describing EME as boosting learning efficiency by forging a closer connection to value differences while maintaining fidelity [N4-R2]. This suggests that value-based exploration guidance is a recurring theme.

Sample efficiency and convergence behavior have improved in recent work. DISCOVER is reported to solve substantially more challenging tasks than previous exploration strategies and to demonstrate significant improvements in sample efficiency compared to state-of-the-art goal selection strategies [N1-F1]. STO-RL achieves faster convergence, higher success rates, and shorter trajectories than prior offline goal-conditioned and hierarchical RL baselines, with ablation studies showing robustness to noisy LLM-generated subgoals [N5-F4]. The evidence also indicates that recent exploration methods are increasingly grounded in theoretical analysis, such as DISCOVER’s formal link to UCB sampling and the analysis of the time until the target task becomes achievable [N1-F1]. This suggests that the field is moving toward more principled exploration that can both improve practical performance and provide tighter convergence guarantees.

Overall, the strongest recent progress appears to be the combination of goal-directed exploration with intrinsic motivation, uncertainty-aware goal selection, and reward shaping, especially in long-horizon and sparse-reward settings. The most effective methods are those that explicitly structure exploration around subgoals, temporal order, or intrinsic curiosity while maintaining theoretical grounding and practical efficiency [N1-F1][N5-F4][N6-R1].

Recent progress in constrained reinforcement learning and proactive constraint handling is moving away from purely overriding safety filters or rigidly joint reward-cost optimization toward more modular, adaptive, and predictive approaches. The core idea is to reduce constraint violations while preserving task performance and exploration, often through action scaling, cost-aware regulators, or predictive safety signals.

Recent methods model and prioritize constraints in RL by integrating constraint prediction into the policy loop rather than simply penalizing violations at the end of an episode. The most notable recent framework is Constraint-Aware Reinforcement Learning via Adaptive Action Scaling, which proposes a modular cost-aware regulator that scales the agent’s actions based on predicted constraint violations. This regulator is trained to minimize constraint violations while avoiding degenerate suppression of actions, and it preserves exploration through smooth action modulation rather than overriding the policy [N2-F2]. Another important direction is safe exploration versus constrained RL: safe exploration methods typically rely on prior knowledge of system dynamics and safe states to construct control barrier functions or predictive shields, while constrained RL allows the agent to learn reward and cost signals online without requiring such prior knowledge [N2-F2]. The evidence also notes that CMDPs are the standard theoretical formulation for constrained RL, emphasizing expected reward maximization while satisfying constraints on expected cost return [N2-R5].

The trade-offs between performance, safety, and constraint satisfaction are clear. Jointly optimizing reward and cost can cause instability, conflicting gradients, and poor performance, as prior work has shown that constrained RL methods often struggle to balance reward and cost within a single policy [N2-F2]. Safe exploration methods can be effective but are limited by the need for prior knowledge of system dynamics and feasible safe states [N2-F2]. In contrast, constraint-aware adaptive action scaling preserves exploration while reducing violations, but it must still balance conservativeness against task-directed behavior [N2-F2]. The evidence also highlights that constraint satisfaction can be made more robust by using feedback-based approaches, as shown by RLSF, which significantly outperforms baselines in reward and safety across environments [N7-R5]. Taken together, the trade-off is between strict safety guarantees and the ability to explore and learn effectively, with recent work favoring predictive, adaptive, and feedback-informed approaches over rigid overrides [N2-F2][N7-R5].

Proactive or predictive constraint handling is becoming standard practice in several ways. First, constraint prediction is embedded into the policy loop through cost-aware regulators that anticipate future constraint violations [N2-F2]. Second, methods are increasingly designed to operate without prior system knowledge, which is a key advantage for early learning stages or unknown-dynamics tasks [N2-F2]. Third, the evidence indicates that constraint-aware methods are being integrated into standard off-policy RL pipelines such as SAC and TD3, which is a practical sign that proactive constraint handling is being embedded into mainstream RL architecture [N2-F2]. Finally, the emphasis on feedback-based safety methods suggests that constraint handling is moving from purely model-based or static prediction toward dynamic, adaptive responses [N7-R5]. While proactive constraint handling is still not universally standardized, the evidence indicates it is becoming the dominant paradigm for safe RL.

In summary, recent constrained RL research is prioritizing adaptive prediction, modular safety enforcement, and feedback-informed control over rigid joint optimization or external overrides. The most effective methods are those that predict constraint violations, scale actions conservatively, and preserve exploration, with proactive predictive handling increasingly standard in the field [N2-F2][N7-R5].

Recent trajectory-planning research in the evidence base is increasingly informed by reinforcement learning (RL) as a way to model planning as sequential decision-making under uncertainty, sparse rewards, and long horizons. The literature appears to model trajectory planning in several ways: as a goal-directed or subgoal-guided search over possible paths, as an informative exploration problem where the planner actively selects informative observations or subgoals, and as a real-time or fast planning problem that can be adapted to complex environments. The cited papers include real-time UAV trajectory planning and tracking using deep RL and adaptive nonlinear methods [N3-R1], informative trajectory planning for field exploration using RL [N3-R2], a fast trajectory planner with RL-based motion planning stages [N3-R3], space trajectory planning with an AlphaZero-inspired RL algorithm for hybrid discrete-continuous action spaces [N3-R4], and deep RL-based trajectory real-time planning for autonomous vehicles [N3-R5]. These examples suggest that trajectory planning is being modeled as a dynamic decision process where the agent must balance reachability, informativeness, temporal structure, and adaptability to uncertain or partially observable environments.

Several RL techniques are improving planning robustness, efficiency, and adaptability. Goal-conditioned and hierarchical RL are prominent because they decompose long-horizon tasks into subgoals or high-level planning stages, allowing planners to guide low-level execution toward long-term objectives while reducing the complexity of direct exploration [N5-F4]. The evidence also emphasizes potential-based reward shaping as a way to turn sparse terminal rewards into temporally consistent dense signals, which helps trajectory planners make progress toward subgoals without being stuck in suboptimal local optima [N5-F4]. Another recurring theme is temporal structure and subgoal order: STO-RL leverages LLM-guided subgoal temporal order and state-to-subgoal-stage mappings to create a structured planning sequence, which improves convergence and success rates in offline sparse-reward settings [N5-F4]. This suggests that planners are becoming more robust by incorporating explicit temporal dependencies and structured exploration.

The evidence also points to adaptability through external planning aids. One paper explicitly uses LLMs alongside RL to facilitate learning from the environment, indicating that planners are increasingly combining model-based reasoning with reinforcement learning to handle complex, open-ended planning problems [N5-R5]. Similarly, the informative trajectory-planning paper implies that planners are designed to actively select informative paths that optimize exploration or field coverage, rather than simply following a fixed policy [N3-R2]. Taken together, these methods improve planning efficiency by reducing the need for brute-force exploration, and they improve adaptability by allowing planners to adjust to sparse reward signals and uncertain environments through structured subgoals, reward shaping, and external reasoning.

Exploration and constraint handling translate into better planning behavior by explicitly guiding the planner toward useful states or actions and by preventing unsafe or suboptimal exploration. In the sparse-reward context, goal-conditioned exploration and curiosity-driven methods help the planner discover useful intermediate progress even when rewards are sparse [N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R5]. In constrained settings, proactive constraint handling through action scaling and cost-aware regulators preserves exploration while reducing violations, which is directly useful for planning because it avoids unsafe maneuvers or premature termination [N2-F2]. The evidence further suggests that constraint-aware methods are being integrated into standard off-policy RL pipelines such as SAC and TD3, which makes them practical for planning tasks that require both safety and flexibility [N2-F2]. Therefore, exploration and constraint handling improve planning by making the planner more efficient, safer, and better able to recover from sparse feedback.

Overall, recent trajectory-planning insights show a shift from purely reactive policy lookup to structured, subgoal-based, and temporally aware planning. The most directly useful techniques are goal-conditioned and hierarchical planning, reward shaping, temporal subgoal ordering, and LLM-augmented planning [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R5][N5-F4][N5-R5]. These methods improve robustness by reducing exploration burden, improve efficiency through structured credit assignment and dense reward signals, and improve adaptability by enabling real-time or dynamic adjustments to the planning process [N5-F4][N5-R5].

Theoretical and practical implications for trajectory planning from sparse-reward and constrained RL are substantial. First, the most directly useful RL principles are those that combine exploration efficiency with safety guarantees: intrinsic motivation, curiosity-driven learning, uncertainty-aware exploration, and constraint-aware action scaling [N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R5][N2-F2]. In sparse-reward settings, these principles help planners find useful intermediate progress when rewards are rare, while in constrained settings they prevent unsafe or constraint-violating actions that could derail the planning process [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The evidence also highlights the importance of value-based exploration guidance and potential-based reward shaping, which connect exploration more directly to the structure of the reward landscape and improve learning efficiency [N4-R2][N5-F4].

Recent research changes the design of planners for uncertainty, long horizons, and safety in several ways. For uncertainty, planners are moving toward structured exploration, goal conditioning, and subgoal decomposition rather than relying on naive random exploration. Goal-conditioned methods such as DISCOVER and STO-RL explicitly model the direction toward the target task, while hierarchical and subgoal methods decompose long-horizon tasks into manageable pieces [N1-F1][N5-F4]. For long horizons, the literature increasingly uses temporal subgoal structures, LLM-guided ordering, and offline RL with dense reward shaping to propagate credit and avoid the vanishing reward problem [N5-F4][N5-R5]. For safety, constraint-aware methods such as adaptive action scaling and cost-aware regulators provide predictive, non-overriding safety enforcement, which preserves exploration while reducing constraint violations [N2-F2]. The evidence also indicates that these methods are being integrated into standard off-policy pipelines, suggesting a shift from isolated safety modules to embedded safety design [N2-F2].

A major practical implication is that trajectory planning must now be designed around the interplay between exploration and constraint enforcement. In sparse-reward settings, planners need to balance the need to explore useful subgoals with the need to avoid wasting samples on unpromising paths. In constrained settings, planners must trade off performance against constraint satisfaction and risk of unsafe exploration. This is exactly the kind of trade-off that recent joint sparse-reward/constraint methods are trying to resolve, though the evidence notes that these approaches still face instability, conflicting gradients, and difficulty in balancing reward and cost within a single policy [N5-F4][N2-F2]. The practical implication is therefore that planners must be designed with modular, adaptive components rather than relying on rigid joint optimization, and that planning performance depends heavily on how well these components can coordinate exploration, subgoal discovery, and constraint prediction [N2-F2][N5-F4].

The remaining practical limitations for deploying these methods in planning tasks are clear. One limitation is the reliance on structured subgoals or external planning aids such as LLMs, which can be brittle when the generated subgoals are imperfect or noisy [N5-F4][N5-R5]. Another limitation is the difficulty of modeling temporal dependencies and subgoal consistency in offline or sparse-reward settings, which is why recent work emphasizes temporal ordering and reward shaping [N5-F4]. A further limitation is the tension between sample efficiency and safety guarantees: while constraint-aware methods reduce violations, they can also suppress exploration too much if the penalty is too strong, and vice versa for exploration-focused methods [N2-F2][N1-F1]. The evidence also suggests that these methods are still being evaluated primarily in controlled or benchmarked settings, so their deployment in real-world planning tasks may depend on robustness to noisy, partial, or delayed feedback [N5-F4][N4-R2]. Overall, the most important practical takeaway is that recent RL research is making trajectory planning more efficient and safer, but deployment still depends on careful handling of uncertainty, long-horizon credit assignment, and the trade-offs between exploration, performance, and constraint satisfaction [N4-R2][N5-F4][N2-F2].
